```{r}
#| include: false
#| cache: false
#| eval: false

library(tidyverse)     # ggplot, dplyr, and friends
library(sf)            # Handle spatial data in R in a tidy way
library(tigris)        # Access geographic data from the US Census
library(tidygeocoder)  # Automated geocoding
library(osrm)          # Access OSRM through R
library(ggrepel)       # Nicer non-overlapping labels
library(glue)          # Easier string interpolation
library(scales)        # Nicer labeling functions
library(patchwork)     # Combine plots nicely
library(ggspatial)     # Nicer map features like scale bars

# Custom ggplot theme to make pretty plots
# Get the font at https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Overpass
theme_roadtrip <- function() {
  theme_void(base_family = "Overpass Light") +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(family = "Overpass", face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      strip.text = element_text(
        family = "Overpass ExtraBold", face = "plain",
        size = rel(1.1), hjust = 0.5),
      plot.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#fffef5", color = NA),
      panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "#fffef5", color = NA)
    )
}


us_states <- states(resolution = "20m", year = 2022, cb = TRUE)

lower_48 <- us_states %>% 
  filter(!(NAME %in% c("Alaska", "Hawaii", "Puerto Rico")))

summer_trips <- tribble(
  ~city, ~state,
  "Northfield", "MN",
  "Fish Creek", "WI",
  "Ames", "IA",
  "Nashville", "TN", 
  "Ocean City", "MD"
)

trips_geocoded <- summer_trips %>% 
  geocode(city = city, state = state, method = "osm") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("long", "lat"), crs = st_crs("EPSG:4326"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig.height: 3
#| fig.width: 5
#| eval: false
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = lower_48) +
  geom_sf(data = trips_geocoded) +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = trips_geocoded,
    aes(label = city, geometry = geometry),
    stat = "sf_coordinates", seed = 1234,
    size = 3, min.segment.length = 0
  ) +
  coord_sf(crs = st_crs("ESRI:102003")) +  # Albers
  theme_roadtrip()

```

## Q: Write the equation of the regression line

Step 1: Read the set up on the handout

Step 2: Which of the following is the correct equation of the regression line?

<br>

::: {.conceptest}
1. $y = 520.1  - 18.7x$

1. $\widehat{y} = 520.1  - 18.7x$

1. $y = -18.7 + 520.1x$

1. $\widehat{y} = -18.7 + 520.1x$
:::

## Q: Interpret the slope in context

::: {.conceptest}
1. For every one-hour increase in sleep duration, the model predicts an average decrease of 18.7 milliseconds in reaction time.

1. For every one-millisecond decrease in reaction time, the model predicts an average increase of 18.7 hours of sleep.

1. If a student gets 0 hours of sleep, their reaction time is predicted to be -18.7 milliseconds.

1. Getting more sleep causes a person's reaction time to drop by exactly 18.7 milliseconds every night.
:::


## Q: Interpret the intercept in context

::: {.conceptest}
1. Yes; it represents the average reaction time (520.1 ms) for all participants in the study regardless of how much they slept.

1. Yes; it represents the predicted reaction time (520.1 ms) for a participant who gets 0 hours of sleep.

1. No; while it represents the predicted reaction time for 0 hours of sleep, this is an example of extrapolation because 0 hours was outside the observed range of 3–9 hours.

1. No; the intercept is just a mathematical placeholder and never carries physical meaning in social science statistics.
:::

## Q: Make a prediction

The researchers are asked to predict the reaction time for a healthy young adult who sleeps 10 hours per night. Using the regression equation  
$\widehat{y}=520.1−18.7x$, which of the following is the most statistically sound conclusion?

::: {.conceptest}
1. The prediction is 333.1 ms; this is highly reliable because 10 hours is very close to the studied range.

1. The prediction is 333.1 ms, but it is unreliable because we cannot assume the linear trend continues beyond the 3–9 hour range.

1. The model cannot be used at all because 10 hours of sleep is biologically impossible for a young adult.

1. The slope would likely change from negative to positive at 10 hours, making the reaction time 520.1 + 18.7(10).
:::


## Q: Purpose of randomization


Why did the researchers randomly assign the 65 participants to specific sleep conditions (3–9 hours) rather than just letting them sleep as much as they usually do?

::: {.conceptest}
1. To ensure that the participants in the 3-hour group were already "short sleepers" who are used to exhaustion.

1. To make the sample size in each sleep condition exactly equal, which is a requirement for linear regression.

1. To balance out potential confounding variables (like caffeine intake or baseline fitness) across the different sleep groups.

1. To increase the "power" of the study by ensuring the results can be generalized to the entire U.S. population.
:::


## Q: Generalizing results

Can the results of this specific study be generalized to all young adults in the United States?

::: {.conceptest}
1. Yes; because the study used a controlled laboratory setting and random assignment, the results apply to everyone.

1. Yes; because the age range (18–25) is a standard definition for "young adults" across the country.

1. No; because the 65 participants were "recruited" (likely a convenience sample from one college), they may not represent the diversity of all U.S. young adults.

1. No; the sample size of 65 is mathematically too small to ever represent a population as large as the United States.
:::


# Regression in Stat 230

## Simple Linear Regression Model

$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$ where $\varepsilon_i \overset{\rm iid}{\sim} N (0, \sigma^2)$

```{r}
#| fig.height: 3.5
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.align: center
library(ggdist)

bike_lm <- lm(rides ~ temp_actual, data = bikes)
bike_dsn <- data.frame(
  temp_actual = c(50, 60, 70, 80),
  yhat = predict(bike_lm, data.frame(temp_actual = c(50, 60, 70, 80))),
  resid_sd = rep(sigma(bike_lm), 4)
)


ggplot(data = bikes, aes(x = temp_actual, y = rides)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.5, color = "#003069") +
  geom_lm(color = "#f15a31") +
  stat_slab(aes(x = temp_actual, ydist = "norm", arg1 = yhat, arg2 = resid_sd), data = bike_dsn, alpha = 0.4, inherit.aes = FALSE, scale = 0.6, fill = "#f15a31") +
  # theme_classic() +
  xlab("Temperature") +
  ylab("No. rides")
```

## Simple Linear Regression Model

$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i$ where $\varepsilon_i \overset{\rm iid}{\sim} N (0, \sigma^2)$

<br>

-   Linear relationship between $x$ and $y$
-   Errors are independent and identically distributed (iid)
-   Errors are normally distributed
-   Errors have mean 0
-   Variance of the errors doesn't depend on $x$

## Notation

Mean function:

$\quad E(Y|X)=\mu\{Y|X\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$

<br>

Fitted model equation:

$\quad \widehat{Y}_i = \widehat{\mu}\{Y|X\} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i$
